extracted.intended_audience: aspiring newspaper reporters and journalism students (particularly sports reporters and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing sports news: types of sporting stories, purposes and ethical considerations, recommended treatment and style, staffing/assignment practices, and related advice for reporting major scientific/astronomical events for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of sporting news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting news stories may be divided into three classes: (1) those that deal with the contestants and the conditions before the event, (2) those that report the contest itself, and (3) those that analyze the event and its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that discuss relative merits and forecast results are based on first-hand observations of the writer or others regarding previous showings and practice. General and detailed accounts of a contest can only be written by writers who have witnessed it. Analysis may be based on the reporter's own observations or on reports printed in newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter familiarity with sport and contestants
rubrics_metrics.description: All sporting news stories can best be written by men who are thoroughly familiar with the sport itself and with the contestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity enables accurate pre-event discussion, credible play-by-play accounts, and informed analysis. This supports depth in forecasting, interpretation, and human-interest development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: satisfy legitimate interest and consider social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The general aim of sporting news stories should be to satisfy a normal, healthy interest in legitimate sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and editors should consider criticisms that newspapers have stimulated excessive interest (e.g., professional baseball, intercollegiate football, prize fighting) and the evil effects on schoolboy and college athletes of undue publicity. Balance reader demand with ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and fairness are as vital to news stories of sports as to any other news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when local readers favor particular contestants, writers are not justified in slighting or treating opponents unfairly. The spirit of fair play essential to sport should be reflected in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment: review and analysis require observation and clear exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The review of conditions preceding the contest and the analysis of the game and of its results require careful observation, clear thinking, and a good expository style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sort of interpretation is similar to editorial and critical writing; it depends on thoughtful synthesis of facts and explanation rather than mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment: event accounts demand spirited narrative and description
rubrics_metrics.description: The account of the event itself demands spirited narrative and description that portrays not only the scenes but the spirit of the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between the emotions of victors and the vanquished, and exploit human-interest elements (personal stories of players). Portray 'heroic' qualities when appropriate to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: variety, originality, and readable English
rubrics_metrics.description: The very popularity of a subject that demands much writing on the same or similar material day by day necessitates variety of presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constant repetition, cheap humor, and almost unintelligible jargon. Strive for picturesque diction and original figures of speech where appropriate, but maintain readable stories in good English with originality comparable to other well-written news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing and assignment for sporting coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Most papers have a special staff of sports writers under the direction of the sporting editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To furnish readers with a very large amount of reading matter about major and minor sports, newspapers dedicate specialized staff. For big events, a paper frequently assigns two men to report it — one to write a general account and one a detailed story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment structure for big events (two-man coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In covering a big sporting event, a newspaper frequently assigns two men to report it, one to write a general account and one a detailed story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows simultaneous production of a broad narrative (spirit, context, human interest) and a detailed play-by-play or box-score style account that requires the writer to have witnessed the contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/astronomical event reporting: precise observational detail and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting astronomical events (e.g., eclipses) include precise times of contacts and durations (to the second), names and roles of observers, photographic evidence, and descriptions of instruments and methods used (e.g., 40-foot photoheliograph, exposure duration, clock mechanism for time exposures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report measured discrepancies (e.g., arrived ten seconds ahead, lasted thirteen seconds less than predicted). Explain how instruments work (mirror, lens, slit, exposure technique) and give concrete numbers (distances, diameters) to help readers understand the phenomenon. Where photographs are used, note who took them and how prints were obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain underlying phenomena for reader comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accessible scientific explanations (e.g., why a total eclipse is possible: apparent diameters due to differing distances) using concrete figures and simple principles (the ocular principle: nearer objects appear larger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies and numeric comparisons (sun diameter, moon diameter, distances) so lay readers grasp why phenomena occur; describe visible effects (e.g., 'a brilliant ring around the circumference of the moon') to connect explanation to observed imagery.
